title: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth
paragraphs: On 18 November 2026, at 2:16 a.m. Pacific time, NASA's Voyager 1 passed an unusual landmark: it is now one light-day from Earth, roughly 25.9 billion kilometres away. To put that into perspective, sunlight needs only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon and about four hours to reach Neptune. The probe is about 20 hours of light-travel time beyond Neptune's distance.

Because of this distance, communication is slow. A command sent from Earth takes a day to arrive, and the reply takes another day, which is why engineers confirmed the milestone from the carrier signal and trajectory calculations. Suzanne Dodd, the project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said: "We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly."

The achievement comes with a warning, however. NASA says it has received no science or engineering data since 14 November, even though the carrier signal is still arriving, and the team is investigating the cause. Power is another constraint: each probe loses about four watts per year, so engineers switched off three devices and replaced them with lower-power alternatives. This should allow the current instruments to keep working until at least the spacecraft's 50th launch anniversary next summer, but Voyager 1 will eventually fall silent.

questions.q: What comparison does the article make with Neptune?
questions.a: Sunlight needs about four hours to reach Neptune, and Voyager 1 is about 20 hours further.

questions.q: How did engineers confirm the milestone?
questions.a: With the carrier signal and trajectory calculations.

questions.q: What did engineers do to save power?
questions.a: They switched off three devices and used lower-power alternatives.
